idiom_name: PORO state machine with the observer gem, or state_machines for the transition table
implementation_notes: Ruby expresses the pattern as a plain object: attr_reader :state, a dispatch(event) method with case/when calling one transition per event, and subscribers added either through the observer gem's Observable#add_observer and #notify_observers or through simple blocks. There is no in-process UI stream - Ruby's UI is server-rendered - so the state reaches the user through whatever the stack provides (Turbo Streams or ActionCable broadcast, a rendered partial), and the transition table itself can be declared with the state_machines gem instead of a hand-written case. That is the whole structure written by hand, so the honest classification is manual rather than library.
pitfalls: The observer gem is no longer part of the standard library (removed in Ruby 3.0 and shipped as a gem), so it is a Gemfile dependency rather than 'just use stdlib'.
notify_observers fires only after changed is called, and an exception from one observer aborts notification of the rest - wrap each subscriber when one failure must not break the fan-out.
Blocks registered as observers capture their surrounding context; in a long-lived server process they keep objects alive unless removed with delete_observer.
State hashes are mutable: freezing the state or using a value object prevents a subscriber from mutating shared state behind the component's back.
